newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Bond issue to stabilise Sri Lanka rates -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bond issue to stabilise Sri Lanka rates -analysts.

text.p: The issue of treasury bonds later this month by Sri Lanka will take the country's interest rates towards a more stable era, analysts said on Wednesday.
The Central Bank said it will begin issuing two-year treasury bonds on February 27 as the first step towards filling an urgent need for transferable long-term securities.
"We will start with a two-year treasury bond. The first auction will be on February 27, and the issue on March 3," said a Central Bank official, who declined to be identified.

Auctions are to be held every two weeks for 500 million rupees ($8.7 million) each time, with interest rates based on a coupon rate of 15 percent. The issue will be underwritten by the state-run Employees Provident Fund.
Analysts in Sri Lanka, which has long suffered from a lack of transferable long-term debt securities, said the move would stabilise interest rates.
"It is good to see the government cut its dependence on short-term debt because it will also help to stabilise interest rates," said Azra Jafferjee, economist at Jardine Fleming.

Sri Lanka has three, six and 12-month treasury bills that are traded in the secondary market. Government securities of two-year, five to six-year and seven to eight-year maturities are not traded as they are mostly issued to state institutions.

"The government, which has had little alternative but to fund heavy spending through treasury bills, can cut the intake of one-year bills when treasury bonds are issued," said Mangala Boyagoda, treasury manager at Union Bank.
Government spending rose sharply in the last two years along with the benchmark 12-month treasury bill yield, as the state funded a ballooning defence bill and a costly wheat flour subsidy.
The average 12-month treasury bill yields in 1995 and 1996 were 17.03 percent and 16.66 percent.
The first jump in state spending was in 1995 when the government decided to modernise its military, which is fighting Tamil Tiger rebels in a civil war that is now in its 14th year.

Defence spending overshot the budget by about nine billion rupees ($158 million) a year in 1995 and 1996. The Central Bank recently said it expected defence estimates of 44 billion rupees ($771 million) for 1997 to be maintained since the capital expenditure needs of the military had been met.
Spending on the wheat subsidy was cut in 1996 by raising the retail price of a kilo (2.2 lb) of flour by five rupees (nine cents) to 16.95 rupees (30 cents).

"The treasury bond issue will compliment the Central Bank's recent relaxation of monetary policy, and help to keep interest rates stable," said an American Express bank dealer who declined to be identified.
The Central Bank cut the reserve requirement on local currency deposits by one percent to 14 percent, and permitted exporters to borrow in foreign currency in early January.
Jardine Fleming's Jafferjee, however, said inflation could be the main obstacle to the Central Bank keeping rates low.
"I do not expect a reduction in the treasury bill rate if inflation rises," she said.
Annualised inflation, which was 15.9 percent in 1996, was at 16.4 percent in January, she said.
